A rough estimate of how many times the inventory was "sold" can be approximated by dividing total sales by the ending inventory balance, which yields roughly 7.6 times ($94,943M / $12,483M). However, strictly speaking, this is a proxy rather than a precise financial metric because the denominator represents only the stock at period-end and does not account for the cost of goods sold or the average inventory level which would provide a more accurate turnover figure. Furthermore, for large diversified corporations like Johnson & Johnson, inventory management strategies can vary significantly across segments (e.g., pharmaceuticals vs. consumer health), meaning that a single aggregate inventory figure may not fully capture the nuances of conventional inventory management effectiveness for the entire entity. Therefore, while the sales-to-inventory ratio suggests the company moved its stock roughly 7 to 8 times during the year, relying solely on this metric without cost of goods sold data limits its precision as a measure of operational efficiency compared to companies with more homogeneous product lines.
